q: You plan a compass check by amplitude at sunrise on the ARC route. At which moment do you take the Sun's bearing?
a: Lower limb half a diameter above the visible horizon
o: Lower limb just touching the visible horizon
Upper limb just clearing the visible horizon
Sun's centre about 5° above the visible horizon
why: The amplitude is for the Sun's centre on the celestial horizon: with refraction and dip, the lower limb then shows about half a diameter up.

fig.title: Sunrise amplitude
lines: Clear eastern horizon, light trade wind

q: You check the steering compass by the Sun's amplitude at sunrise. What is the compass error?
why: sin Amp = sin 20°46′ / cos 17° → Amp E21.8°S, true bearing 111.8°; error = true − compass = 111.8° − 118° = 6°W.

fig.title: Sunrise, 25 November
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

q: You are on the Pacific Puddle Jump and take an amplitude at sunset. What true bearing do you compare with the compass?
why: sin Amp = sin 8°11′ / cos 12° → Amp 8.4°, from west toward the Dec's name (N): 270° + 8° = 278°T.

fig.title: Sunset, 10 April
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

q: You want to catch the sunrise for an amplitude. Where on the horizon do you look for the Sun?
a: About 065° — 25° north of east
o: About 115° — 25° south of east
About 067° — 23° north of east
About 090° — due east in winter
why: The Sun rises toward the name of its Dec in either hemisphere: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 20° → E25°N, about 065°.

q: You take an amplitude at sunset to check the compass. Which true bearing do you use?
a: 270°T, whatever your latitude
o: 270°T, but only on the equator
302°T — 270° plus the latitude
238°T — 270° minus the latitude
why: With Dec 0° sin Amp = 0: at the equinox the Sun's centre sets due west, 270°T, in any latitude.

fig.title: Sunset, 20 March
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

q: You check the steering compass by amplitude on your present heading. What deviation do you log?
why: Amp W23.4°S → 246.6°T; error 246.6° − 255° = 8°W; deviation = error − variation = 8°W − 11°W = 3°E.

q: You take a sunrise amplitude on the way to the Azores. What is the Sun's true bearing?
why: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 38° → Amp 30.3°, east toward N: 090° − 30° = 060°T. The higher the latitude, the bigger the amplitude.

fig.title: Sunrise, 21 June
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

q: You take the Sun's bearing mid-morning for a compass check. Which true azimuth do you compare it with?
why: Zn = atan2(−cos Dec sin LHA, cos Lat sin Dec − sin Lat cos Dec cos LHA) = 127°; LHA over 180° puts the Sun in the east.

q: You check the compass by the Sun's azimuth on your way to Antigua. What is the deviation on this heading?

fig.title: Afternoon sun, 1 December
lines: Sun bears 246°C over the steering compass

q: You want the Sun's azimuth for a compass check today. Which of these times do you choose?
a: 0730 — the Sun is low, its bearing easy to take
o: 1145 — the Sun is high and bright to sight
1215 — just after noon, the Sun is steady
Any of them — the azimuth is computed anyway
why: A high Sun is hard to bear accurately and near noon in the tropics its bearing swings fast: take the azimuth with the Sun low.

q: Bound for Cape Town, you use HO 249 for the Sun's azimuth to check the compass. What Zn do you take?
why: South latitude, LHA less than 180°: Zn = 180° + Z = 180° + 97° = 277°T.

q: At evening twilight you take Sirius over the steering compass. What deviation do you log for this heading?

fig.title: Evening twilight, 15 February
lines: Sirius bears 145°C over the steering compass

q: You check the compass by the Sun's azimuth in the South Atlantic. What is the compass error?
why: LHA = GHA + longitude east = 297°41′ + 6° = 303°41′ → Zn 098°T; error = 098° − 094° = 4°E (compass least, error east).

fig.title: Morning sun, 15 January
lines: DR 25°S 6°E, Cape Town to St Helena
Sun bears 094°C over the steering compass

q: Two days from Saint Lucia you check the steering compass on Polaris. What is the compass error?
a: 3°E — the compass reads low
o: 3°W — the compass reads low
3°E — the compass reads high
3°W — the compass reads high
why: In low latitudes Polaris is within about 1° of true north: error = 000° − 357° = 3°E; the compass reads low.

fig.title: Evening twilight, ARC route
lines: Polaris bears 357° by the steering compass

q: You plan your compass checks for the next week on this passage. Which of these is no use to you here?
a: A bearing of Polaris
o: The Sun's amplitude at sunset
The Sun's azimuth in the morning
The azimuth of a bright star
why: Polaris lies within about 1° of the north celestial pole: south of the equator it is below your horizon.

fig.title: Marquesas to the Tuamotus
lines: Clear nights, sharp horizon at twilight

q: You use Polaris to check the steering compass on this heading. What deviation do you log?
why: Error = 359.2° − 006° = 6.8°W; deviation = error − variation = 6.8°W − 12°W = 5.2°, about 5°E.

fig.title: Polaris check, 40°N
lines: Bermuda to the Azores, evening twilight
Polaris bears 006° by the steering compass

q: Making landfall in the Azores, you steer along this transit. What deviation do you log for this heading?
why: A transit needs no almanac: error = 248° − 252° = 4°W; deviation = error − variation = 4°W − 7°W = 3°E.

q: Crossing the Indian Ocean, the Sun's azimuth this morning gives this compass error on your present heading. What is the deviation?
why: Deviation = error − variation = 6°W − 4°W = 2°W (west counted negative).

q: You have steered this compass course all watch on the ARC. What true course do you plot on the plotting sheet?
why: True = compass + deviation + variation, east +, west −: 263° + 2°E − 16°W = 249°T.

q: In the trades you gybe onto a new heading. What do you now take as the deviation?
a: Unknown until you check it on 200°C
o: 1°E — it was found only this morning
1°W — it reverses after a gybe
0° — deviation is negligible at sea
why: Deviation changes with the ship's head: a value found on 260°C does not hold on 200°C — check again or use the card for that heading.

fig.title: Deviation log, day 6
lines: No check yet on the new heading

q: You load the boat in Las Palmas for the Atlantic crossing. What do you do about the steering compass?
a: Check its deviation again on several headings
o: Use last spring's card — the compass hasn't moved
Allow a flat 5° on every heading for the steel
Rely on the fluxgate — it ignores nearby steel
why: New steel near the compass changes its deviation: move it away if you can, then check the deviation afresh on several headings.

fig.title: Las Palmas, the day before the start
lines: Spare anchor and chain in the cockpit locker
Two dive tanks lashed beside the binnacle
Compass checked and carded last spring

q: You fill in the deviation log on the crossing. What else do you need to find the deviation?
a: The variation at your position
o: The Sun's altitude at the time
The log reading at the time
The height of eye on deck
why: Deviation = error − variation: read the variation for your DR position from the pilot chart or the chart.

q: Crossing westward from the Canaries, you check the compass on the same heading. What does the log tell you?
a: Deviation steady at 1°W; variation changes
o: Deviation growing from 7°W to 16°W
Deviation steady at 1°E; variation changes
The compass is failing and needs a swing
why: Deviation = error − variation: 7 − 6, 12 − 11 and 16 − 15 all give 1°W. The growing error is the variation across the ocean.

q: You need the variation for tonight's compass check. What value do you use?
why: Interpolate between the isogonic lines: 10° + 3/5 × 5° = 13°W.

fig.title: Pilot chart, North Atlantic
lines: Your DR: 3/5 of the way from 10°W to 15°W

q: You take the variation for your compass checks from the chart's compass rose. What do you use?
You fit a new autopilot with a fluxgate compass before an ocean passage and find this. What do you do?
a: Run its calibration turns in calm water, then compare
o: Apply 8° to every heading shown on the fluxgate
Move the steering compass until the two agree
Trust the fluxgate — electronic compasses have no deviation
why: A fluxgate also senses the boat's magnetism: its calibration (slow full circles) compensates it; then check it against the steering compass.

q: With the electrics down for the rest of the passage, what do you steer by?
a: The magnetic steering compass
o: The handheld GPS's COG
The fluxgate on the engine battery
The wind instrument's angle
why: The magnetic steering compass needs no power: keep it lit at night with a torch and keep checking its error.

q: The autopilot shows true heading. What is the steering compass's deviation on this heading?
why: True to magnetic: 253°T + 12°W = 265°M; deviation = magnetic − compass = 265° − 262° = 3°E.

q: You switch on the backup GPS mid-ocean and see this. Why is there no position yet?
a: It needs a fourth satellite to solve its clock error
o: Three satellites give only a line, not a point
It needs one satellite in each quadrant of the sky
It needs six — two for each of three axes
why: Each satellite gives a range from the signal's travel time; with the receiver's clock unknown, three ranges and the clock need four.

fig.title: GNSS status page
lines: Antenna clear of the rig, open sky

q: You plan to enter the lagoon using the plotter. What does this GNSS status tell you?
a: Poor geometry: the fix may be tens of metres out
o: An HDOP over 5 means the fix is good to 5 m
The fix is good; HDOP affects only height
The plotter would warn you of any bad fix
why: HDOP multiplies the range error and bunched satellites give a high HDOP: enter the pass by eye in good light, not by the plotter.

fig.title: Approaching a Tuamotu pass
lines: Satellites used: 5, all low to the north
Pass 150 m wide, reef on both sides

q: You fit this receiver for the ocean passage. What do you gain by leaving all the systems on?
a: More satellites: better geometry, fewer gaps
o: A separate datum for each system
An accurate fix without any clock
A fix that cannot be jammed
why: GPS (USA), Galileo (EU), GLONASS (Russia) and BeiDou (China) all give ranges: more satellites mean a lower DOP and more resilience.

q: Approaching the atoll at dusk, the plotter shows you safely 0.4 M off the reef. What do you do?
a: Stand off until daylight: the chart may be a mile out
o: Carry on: GPS is accurate to a few metres
Shift the GPS position 1 M and carry on
Change the plotter's datum and carry on
why: GPS is good to metres, but an old survey can put the reef a mile from where it lies: keep sea room, use radar and your eyes.

fig.title: Chart of a Pacific atoll
lines: Note: positions may be 1 M in error
Plotter: boat 0.4 M from the reef

q: Your old paper chart of a Pacific island uses a local datum and carries this note. Which position do you plot?
why: In south latitude moving north reduces the latitude; in west longitude moving west increases it: 26.40′ − 0.15′, 36.10′ + 0.42′.

q: Bound for the Indian Ocean, you see this at night. What do you do?
a: Treat it as jamming: DR from the last fix, radar, log it
o: Restart all the receivers until one gets a fix
Heave to until the GPS signal comes back
Steer for the last waypoint on the plotter
why: Every receiver losing the fix at once points to jamming: navigate by DR, radar and sights, and report and log the outage.

q: Crossing the Arabian Sea at night, you see this. What do you do?
a: Treat all GNSS as spoofed: DR, radar ranges, sights
o: Trust the GPS position — the log must be fouled
Reboot the plotter and carry on navigating by it
Average the GPS and DR positions and carry on
why: A frozen, plausible position that disagrees with the log and radar is spoofing: navigate independently of GNSS and report it.

fig.title: Gulf of Oman approach, 0200
lines: AIS: two ships shown at an airport ashore
Radar: coast 12 M off, not as on the plotter

q: Halfway across the Atlantic, the receiver shows this. How far can you trust the position?
a: To within about 10 m — ample for the ocean
o: Only to about a mile without SBAS
To 1 cm — SBAS is no longer needed
Not at all until SBAS comes back
why: SBAS (EGNOS, WAAS) corrects only within its service area; plain GPS with a good HDOP is good to metres — ample offshore.

q: On passage from the Bahamas to Beaufort, North Carolina, you receive this warning. What do you plan?
a: A good fix before, then DR, and the sextant ready
o: Nothing — the warning is for ships, not yachts
Reset the receiver at 1300 to clear the fault
Steer by GPS COG, which is not affected
why: In an outage window, start DR from a known fix, keep the log and compass courses, and check with sights or radar.

fig.title: NAVAREA IV warning
lines: GPS testing: signals may be unreliable

q: Crossing the doldrums at night, what do you do with the handheld GPS and the spare VHF?
a: Put them in the oven, disconnected
o: Plug them into ship's power to stay charged
Keep them on deck in the grab bag
Switch them on to log the position
why: A strike can kill everything wired to the boat: a closed metal box like the oven shields unconnected spares as a Faraday cage.

fig.title: ITCZ, 0100
lines: Lightning every few seconds, 2–3 M off
Handheld GPS and VHF on the chart table

q: You find this on the watch log. What is the most likely fault?
a: The shared GPS antenna or its cable
o: The whole GPS system is down
The plotter's chart card has failed
The AIS transponder is being jammed
why: The handheld has a fix, so the satellites are fine; plotter and AIS share one antenna, so check it and its cable first.

q: You review the boat's systems before a 3,000-mile passage. What is the best change?
a: Give the DSC VHF its own GPS and carry a handheld
o: Add a second plotter on the same antenna
Fit a bigger house battery bank instead
Carry a spare antenna cable, nothing else
why: One antenna and one battery feed everything, even the DSC distress position: add an independent source and a handheld.

fig.title: Navigation wiring
lines: One GPS antenna on the stern arch
It feeds plotter, AIS, autopilot, DSC VHF
All on one house battery bank

q: You check the grab bag before leaving the Canaries. What do you add for the handheld GPS?
a: Spare lithium batteries, sealed in the bag
o: A charging lead for the ship's 12 V
A paper chart of the destination
Nothing — it lasts weeks on one set
why: There is no charging in the raft: a tested handheld GPS with sealed spare batteries gives your position to rescuers.

fig.title: Ocean grab bag check
lines: Handheld VHF, flares, water, first-aid kit
Handheld GPS in a waterproof pouch

q: Mid-Atlantic, your family sees your AIS position online. How does it reach them?
a: Satellites pick up your AIS signal and relay it
o: Ships within VHF range relay it by DSC
Your AIS sends it by HF radio every hour
Your EPIRB transmits it every six hours
why: Satellites in orbit receive AIS transmissions and pass them ashore; ships still see you only within VHF range, some 20 M.

fig.title: Message from home, day 9
lines: Family: 'We see you on a tracking website'
Nearest ship on your AIS: none for 2 days

q: Mid-ocean, how do you get the next GRIB file?
a: Request a small GRIB by email over the Iridium link
o: Download it by VHF from the nearest coast station
Receive it on NAVTEX at 518 kHz
Wait for the GPS to update the forecast
why: Iridium covers the whole globe: a small compressed GRIB by email arrives in minutes; NAVTEX and VHF reach only near the coast.

fig.title: Weather at sea
lines: Need: GRIB for the next 5 days

q: You plan this high-latitude summer passage. What do you do about communications?
a: Add Iridium: Inmarsat's satellites sit over the equator
o: Keep Inmarsat alone: it covers the whole globe
Rely on VHF DSC: it reaches satellites overhead
Rely on NAVTEX: it carries email up there
why: Inmarsat's geostationary satellites sit low on the horizon and are lost beyond about 75° of latitude; Iridium's polar orbits cover the poles.

fig.title: Summer passage to Svalbard
lines: Route north of 75°N for two weeks

q: You check the EPIRB before the Atlantic crossing. What must you do?
a: Register it to you and this boat
o: Nothing — it sends your position anyway
Test it with a full activation in harbour
Reprogramme it to transmit on 121.5 MHz only
why: Cospas-Sarsat decodes the beacon's ID: the MRCC uses the registration to know the boat, the crew and whom to call ashore.

fig.title: Pre-departure check
lines: 406 MHz EPIRB, came with the boat
Registration: previous owner's name and boat
Battery and hydrostatic release in date

q: You are choosing an EPIRB for an ocean passage. What does model B give you?
a: Your position in its first bursts, within minutes
o: A stronger signal for ships close by
Two-way messages with the MRCC
No need to register the beacon
why: Without GNSS the satellites must work out the position from the signal, more slowly and coarsely; with GNSS it goes out in the alert.

fig.title: Choosing an EPIRB
lines: Model A: 406 MHz, no GNSS receiver
Model B: 406 MHz with built-in GNSS

q: Adrift in the liferaft, how does the search aircraft find you in the last few miles?
a: It homes on the EPIRB's 121.5 MHz signal
o: It follows the 406 MHz position alone
It hears you on VHF channel 16 by itself
It reads your AIS signal by satellite
why: The 406 MHz alert goes via Cospas-Sarsat to the MRCC; the 121.5 MHz homing signal leads aircraft and ships to the raft.

fig.title: Day 3 in the liferaft
lines: Search aircraft heard, not yet seen

q: A crew member asks why the GPS position goes in the logbook every hour. What do you answer?
a: If the GPS fails, DR starts from a recent known position
o: The insurer needs it to settle any claim
The plotter needs it to check its datum
It keeps the GPS receiver calibrated
why: With an hourly position, course and log reading on paper, a GPS failure costs you less than an hour of DR.

fig.title: Skipper's standing orders
lines: Every hour: time, GPS position, log
Noon: sun sight compared with GPS

q: Your crew questions the daily sun sight. What do you tell them?
a: It keeps the skill and the kit ready for a failure
o: It is more accurate than GPS offshore
The almanac must be used once a day
It corrects the GPS for its datum
why: Celestial navigation is the backup: practise it daily and compare with GPS, so you can trust it when the electronics fail.

fig.title: Day 4, GPS working well
lines: Noon sight vs GPS: 1.8 M apart

q: Your only GPS failed after the last hourly entry. What DR position do you plot at 1500?
why: 21 M on 260°: d.lat 3.6′S; departure 20.7′W ÷ cos 15.3° = d.long 21.4′W.

q: You are south of the equator and want a night check on the compass. What do you use where you once used Polaris?
a: The Southern Cross when its long axis is vertical
o: Sigma Octantis, the faint south pole star
Canopus whenever it is in the south
The Pointers at any time of the night
why: With its long axis vertical the Cross is on your meridian and bears 180°T; σ Octantis, at the pole, is too faint to take.

fig.title: Night check, Rio to Cape Town
lines: Clear sky, Southern Cross well up

q: On passage from New Zealand to Tonga you take this bearing of Acrux. What deviation do you log?
why: On the meridian Acrux bears 180°T; error 180° − 165° = 15°E; deviation = error − variation = 15°E − 19°E = 4°W.

fig.title: Night, 33°S 176°E
lines: Southern Cross upside down, low in the south
Acrux on your meridian, below the pole

q: Bound from Tahiti to Rarotonga, you check the steering compass on Canopus, low in the south-east. What deviation do you log?
Bound for Mauritius, you want a star to check the compass tonight. Which one do you take?
a: Acrux — low enough to bear over the compass
o: Sirius — the brightest star in the sky
Canopus — nearly due south, easy to use
Rigel — high and clear of any haze
why: A bearing is good only of a low body: at 60°–80° you cannot hold the compass level and sight the star. Acrux at 19° is right.

q: Bound from Panama to New Zealand, you find the steering compass card tilting and dragging as you go south. Why?
a: It is balanced for the north: magnetic dip pulls it
o: Its fluid is too cold in the southern winter
Variation is too large for it near New Zealand
Its magnets weakened as it crossed the equator
why: A compass card is balanced for one magnetic zone; far south the dip of the field tilts a northern card. Fit a southern or global one.

fig.title: Steering compass, 38°S
lines: Card tilted, sticks on one side
Fine in the Caribbean and on the equator

q: Jupiter is setting over a clear western horizon. At what moment do you take its bearing for an amplitude?
a: With it about a Sun's diameter above the horizon
o: As it touches the visible horizon
With it half a Sun's diameter above the horizon
With it 5° up, well clear of the haze
why: On the celestial horizon, refraction (34′) and dip (3′) lift a point body about 0.6° — one Sun's diameter — above the visible horizon.

fig.title: Jupiter setting
lines: Bright, low over a clear western horizon

q: On the way to the Azores you take the amplitude of Venus as it sets. What true bearing do you use?
why: sin Amp = sin 22°10′ / cos 35° → Amp 27.4°, from west toward N: 270° + 27° = 297°T. Amp ≈ Dec only near the equator.

q: In mid-Atlantic you check the steering compass as Rigel rises. What deviation do you log?
why: sin Amp = sin 8°10′ / cos 30° → E9.4°S, 099.4°T; error 099.4° − 106° = 6.6°W; deviation 6.6°W − 12°W = 5.4°E, about 5°E.

q: Approaching the Western Approaches from the Azores on 21 June, you take a sunrise amplitude. What true bearing do you use?
why: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 50° → Amp 38.2°, from east toward N: 090° − 38° = 052°T. At 50°N the amplitude is far more than the Dec.

fig.title: Sunrise, 21 June
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

q: Bound for Norway, you take the sunrise bearing late, with the Sun's centre about 1° higher than it should be. How far out is your check?
a: About 2½°: the Sun climbs at a slant up here
o: About ¼°: as it would be near the equator
About 1°: one degree for each degree up
None: the Sun rises at a fixed bearing
why: At 58°N the Sun's path is oblique: its Zn goes from 041.4° on the horizon to 043.7° at 1° up; near the equator it would move 0.2°.

fig.title: Sunrise, 21 June, 58°N
lines: Here the Sun takes 11 minutes to climb 1°

q: On the Cape to Rio route you take an amplitude at sunset. What is the compass error?
why: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 33° → W28.3°S, 241.7°T; error = true − compass = 241.7° − 250° = 8°W.

q: You take the Sun's bearing for this compass check. How far out could the azimuth you work for it be?
a: About 3°: near the zenith the bearing swings fast
o: Under 0.1°: the azimuth hardly changes with time
About ½°: 2 minutes is ½° of hour angle
About 1°: as for any Sun on a morning check
why: At 84° up the Sun's Zn goes from 057° to 055° in 2 minutes (LHA 355° → 355.5°); mid-morning it moves under 0.1°. Use a low Sun.

fig.title: Compass check, 15°N
lines: Watch error unknown, up to 2 minutes

q: South of the equator on the Puddle Jump, the Sun is north of you after noon. What is its true azimuth for your compass check?
why: LHA = 150°51.5′ − 131°20′W = 19°31.5′; LHA under 180° puts the Sun west of your meridian: Zn = 327°T, to the north-west.

q: On passage from Fiji to Vanuatu you check the steering compass on the morning Sun. What deviation do you log?

fig.title: Morning sun, west of the date line

q: At evening twilight on the way to the Azores you take Jupiter over the steering compass. What deviation do you log?
On the ARC you use HO 249 Volume 1 for a star's azimuth at dusk. What is the compass error?
why: Volume 1 gives Zn directly for its selected stars: error = true − compass = 091° − 098° = 7°W (the deviation would be 4°E).

q: Mid-ocean, you want a fresh deviation card for the main headings. How do you get it?
a: Steer each heading in turn and bear the Sun on each
o: Take one Sun bearing and apply it to every heading
Compare the compass with the GPS track for a day
Wait for a transit at the landfall to swing it
why: Deviation changes with heading: steer each heading, bear the Sun, work its Zn for that time and log error − variation.

fig.title: Compass swing at sea
lines: Calm sea, clear sky, morning Sun
No land or transit for 1,500 M

q: You swing the compass on four headings between 0900 and 0940. A crew member wants to use the 0900 azimuth for every bearing. What do you tell them?
a: Work an azimuth for each bearing: the Sun moves 7°
o: Fine: the Sun's bearing changes little in 40 minutes
Fine: use the mean azimuth of 133° for all four
Take all four bearings at 0900 on the same heading
why: The Sun's Zn moves 7.3° in those 40 minutes: one azimuth for all would put up to 7° of false deviation into the card.

q: You swing the compass in the Indian Ocean with the morning Sun. What is the deviation on 090°C?
why: On 090°C: error = 066° − 071° = 5°W; deviation = 5°W − 1°W = 4°W. Use each time's own Zn, not the 0800 one.

q: Your new deviation card has the four cardinal headings. What deviation do you apply steering 045°C?
a: About 2°W
o: About 2°E
About 4°W
About 7°W
why: Deviation runs smoothly between headings: halfway from 000°C (2°E) to 090°C (5°W) it is (+2° − 5°) ÷ 2, about 1½–2°W.

q: Your swing at sea shows large deviation on east and west headings. A crew member offers to adjust the corrector magnets now. What do you do?
a: Steer by the card; leave the magnets to an adjuster
o: Turn the correctors until the Sun's bearing agrees
Move the compass to where the error is smallest
Take the correctors out and start again from zero
why: Adjusting at sea without a full swing can make it worse: steer by the card, keep checking, and have it adjusted in port.

q: You check the compass twice on the same heading and get these results. What explains them?
a: Heeling error: heel shifts the boat's magnetism
o: Variation changed with the boat's heel
The Sun's azimuth was worked wrongly once
The compass card sticks when she heels
why: Heel moves the keel, engine and rig relative to the compass: deviation changes with heel as well as heading — log it per tack.

fig.title: Same heading, 240°C
lines: Next day, heeled 20° to port: error 2°W

q: Beating to windward, you go about onto port tack. What true course do you plot?
why: Port-tack deviation 4°W and variation 6°W are both west, so subtract: 310°C − 4° − 6° = 300°T.

q: On the night watch the compass error on the same heading has jumped by 10°. What do you check first?
a: What has been stowed near the compass
o: Whether the variation has changed
Whether the Sun's tables are right
Whether the compass fluid has leaked
why: Steel, magnets or electronics moved near the compass change its deviation at once: move them away, then check again.

fig.title: Compass check, 0400
lines: Crew restowed the cockpit lockers at dusk

q: Six days out of Cape Town you notice you still apply the departure variation. What true course have you been steering?
why: True = compass − westerly variation: 315° − 19°W = 296°T, not the 290°T you planned — 6° to the right of your track.

fig.title: Cape Town to St Helena, day 6

q: A crew member suggests checking the compass against the GPS course over ground instead of the Sun. When is that good enough?
a: Only with no current and no leeway
o: Always: COG is the boat's true heading
Always, if the GPS shows a good HDOP
Never: GPS COG is a magnetic value
why: COG is the track over the ground: current and leeway set it off the heading, so the difference is not the compass error.

fig.title: Mid-Atlantic, day 9
lines: Trade wind F5, 1 kn of current likely
Leeway on a broad reach: unknown

q: Your new satellite compass gives true heading from two GNSS antennas. What is its weak point on an ocean passage?
a: It loses its heading when GNSS is lost or jammed
o: It needs swinging for deviation like a compass
It shows only magnetic heading, never true
It drifts and must be reset each day at noon
why: A GNSS compass needs satellite signals: jamming or an antenna fault kills its heading, so keep the magnetic compass checked.

fig.title: Satellite compass
lines: True heading: no deviation, no variation
Feeds the autopilot and the radar overlay

q: After a wave fills the cockpit, the EPIRB in its bracket starts flashing. What does that mean?
a: It has activated and is sending a distress alert
o: It is running a self-test after getting wet
Its battery is low and needs replacing
It is only showing that its GPS has a fix
why: A water-activated EPIRB switches on when it gets wet in its bracket: the strobe means a 406 MHz distress alert is going out.

q: Your EPIRB has gone off by accident, 900 miles from land. What do you do?
a: Call an MRCC at once and report the false alert
o: Switch it off quietly: no harm has been done
Leave it on until a ship comes to check
Take out its battery and note it in the log
why: A false alert launches a search: switch the beacon off and call an MRCC at once by satphone with its ID, your position and time.

fig.title: False alert, day 12
lines: EPIRB set off by a wave 20 min ago

q: You call the MRCC to cancel your false EPIRB alert. What do they need from you?
a: The beacon's hex ID, boat's name, position and time
o: Only the boat's name and her home port
The EPIRB's make and battery expiry date
Your MMSI and the VHF channel you keep
why: The hex ID matches the alert to your beacon; with the time, position and 'all well', the MRCC can stand the search down.

q: Adrift after abandoning ship, you watch the EPIRB. This blue light comes on. What does it tell you?
a: The system has received your alert and position
o: A rescue unit is now on its way to you
The battery is half used and failing
The beacon has just found a GPS fix
why: Galileo's Return Link Service only confirms that Cospas-Sarsat has your alert and position; it does not mean help is close.

q: In the liferaft, an aircraft flies over and rocks its wings. A crew member wants to switch off the EPIRB to save its battery. What do you do?
a: Leave it on until you are picked up
o: Switch it off now that they have found you
Switch it off and on again every hour
Switch it off until night falls
why: The ship sent to you homes on 121.5 MHz and the 406 MHz position: leave the EPIRB on until you are aboard.

q: At night you have one radar target and one AIS target ahead. What do you navigate by?
a: Radar and your eyes: her AIS position is wrong
o: Her AIS: it is more accurate than radar
The mean of the radar and AIS positions
Her AIS: the radar target is sea clutter
why: AIS shows where the ship's own GPS puts her; when it disagrees with radar and eyes, the AIS may be wrong (Rule 7: no scanty data).

fig.title: Night, 0230, 40 M off Cape Verde
lines: No other target on radar or AIS

q: A ship's compass bearing has been steady for 12 minutes, but her AIS shows a comfortable CPA. What do you do?
a: Treat it as a risk of collision and act early
o: Stand on: the AIS says she passes 1.8 M off
Wait for the AIS CPA to update, then decide
Call her to correct her AIS, then stand on
why: A steady compass bearing means risk of collision (Rule 7); AIS CPA rests on GPS and heading data that may be wrong. Act in ample time.

fig.note: Bearing 040° steady 12 min · AIS CPA 1.8 M

q: A ship calls you on VHF about your AIS. What do you do?
a: Give her your position, then check the AIS's GPS
o: Switch the AIS off for the rest of the passage
Ignore it: ships see you on radar anyway
Re-enter your MMSI so the error clears
why: Your AIS sends its own GPS's position: tell the ship where you are, then check the AIS GPS antenna and its status page.

fig.title: VHF call, mid-Atlantic
lines: Ship: 'Your AIS puts you on Barbados'
Your plotter: 280 M east of Barbados
The AIS transponder has its own GPS

q: You plan to cross ahead of this container ship using her AIS. Where is her bow relative to the AIS position?
a: About 260 m ahead of it
o: At the AIS position itself
About 70 m ahead of it
About 165 m ahead of it
why: AIS reports the position of the ship's GPS antenna; A is the distance from it to the bow, so her bow is 260 m ahead of the dot.

fig.title: AIS target: container ship, 330 m
lines: Static data: A 260, B 70, C 20, D 28 (m)
Plotter draws a dot at her AIS position
Night, she is end-on to you

q: You compare the noon-to-noon runs. What do they tell you?
a: A current of about ¾ kn setting with you
o: A current of about ¾ kn setting against you
A current of about 1½ kn setting with you
A GPS error of about 18 M in the fix
why: 158 M over the ground − 140 M through the water = 18 M in 24 h: a favourable current of 0.75 kn.

fig.title: Noon to noon, day 7
lines: Log checked against GPS in slack water

q: Today's noon latitude is 14 miles from the GPS, after a week of agreement within 2 miles. What do you do first?
a: Recheck the sight: the Dec, index error, arithmetic
o: Navigate by the sextant: the GPS has failed
Average the two and plot 14°29′N
Reset the GPS and accept its next fix
why: A sudden 14′ gap after a week of agreement usually means a slip in the sight — wrong Dec, IE, a misread degree. Check before doubting GPS.

fig.title: Noon, day 8, ARC route
lines: Days 1–7: sight and GPS within 2 M

q: The main GPS and the handheld now disagree by 4 miles. How do you decide which to trust?
a: Check both against your DR, and a sight if you can
o: Trust the main set: it has the bigger antenna
Trust the handheld: it has its own antenna
Plot the mean of the two and carry on
why: Two sources that disagree cannot tell you which is wrong: a third — your DR from log and compass, or a sun line — decides.

q: The GPS loses its fix every time you send email over the satellite terminal. What is the likely cause?
a: The satcom antenna transmits too close to the GPS one
o: The satellites are below the horizon at those times
The email software resets the GPS receiver
The batteries sag under the satcom's load
why: Iridium and Inmarsat transmit just above the GPS L1 band: mount the GPS antenna well away from the satcom one, not level with it.

fig.title: Watch log, day 5
lines: Both antennas on the same pushpit rail

q: You suspect jamming. A crew member wants to set the receiver to Galileo only. Will it help?
a: Little: all the systems share the same L-band
o: Yes: Galileo signals cannot be jammed
Yes: Galileo uses a separate datum
Yes: one system needs fewer satellites
why: GPS, Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou all send weak L-band signals near 1.2–1.6 GHz: a jammer blocks them all. Navigate by DR and radar.

fig.title: GNSS receiver, Red Sea
lines: GPS, Galileo and GLONASS all lost
Signal strength low on every satellite

q: The plotter's boat symbol is still moving, but the status reads 'No fix — DR'. What is the position shown?
a: An estimate from the last fix, COG and SOG
o: A GNSS fix from fewer satellites
A fix from the AIS transponder's GPS
A fix corrected by the SBAS signal
why: Without a fix the plotter dead-reckons on the last COG and SOG: note the time of the last real fix and start your own DR from it.

q: You receive this warning on the way to Antigua. What do you plan for the next day?
a: A fix before it, then DR and sights; expect HF gaps
o: Nothing: space weather affects only aircraft
Switch every receiver off until it passes
Rely on HF weatherfax instead of satellites
why: A geomagnetic storm upsets the ionosphere: GNSS fixes may jump or drop out and HF fades. Keep DR going and the sextant ready.

q: Your Iridium terminal shows no signal tonight. What do you check first?
a: That the antenna has a clear view of the sky
o: That the antenna points towards the equator
That the next satellite pass is due at noon
That the SIM card has not expired
why: Iridium satellites cross the whole sky in low orbits: the antenna needs a clear view overhead. Pointing at the equator is for Inmarsat.

fig.title: Iridium terminal, day 3
lines: Antenna moved under the hard top

q: The Inmarsat terminal drops out on one heading only. What is the likely cause?
a: The mast and sails block its view of the satellite
o: The satellite sets below the horizon at sea
The heel tilts the dome beyond its range
The radar beam jams it on that heading
why: An Inmarsat satellite sits over the equator: with it dead ahead, the mast and mainsail stand between the stern dome and the satellite.

fig.title: Inmarsat dome on the stern arch

q: The satellite phone has died mid-Atlantic. How do you still get the forecast?
a: High-seas bulletins and weatherfax on the SSB
o: NAVTEX, which reaches into mid-ocean
VHF forecasts from the nearest coast station
GRIB files over the GPS receiver
why: Mid-ocean only HF reaches you without a satellite: high-seas forecasts and weatherfax charts on the SSB receiver. NAVTEX reaches ~300 M.

q: Your satcom has failed and your shore contact expects a daily email. What do you do?
a: Ask the ship on VHF to email your shore contact
o: Set off the EPIRB briefly so they see you are well
Send a DSC distress alert, then cancel it
Nothing: they will call the MRCC on day 7 anyway
why: Any ship can relay a routine message; never use an EPIRB or a distress alert for it. Your float plan should say a missed email is no distress.

fig.title: Day 6 of 20, mid-Atlantic
lines: Float plan: daily email by 1800 UT

q: Just south of the equator you get ready for a sunrise amplitude. Where do you expect the Sun to rise?
a: About 105° — 15° south of east
o: About 075° — 15° north of east
About 090° — due east on the equator
About 107° — Dec plus your latitude
why: Near the equator cos Lat ≈ 1, so the amplitude ≈ the Dec: the Sun rises about E15°S, 105°T.

q: The pilot chart shows no variation at your position. What does today's Sun check give you?
a: The deviation on 190°C: 3°E
o: The variation here: 3°E
The deviation on 190°C: 3°W
Nothing until you know the variation
why: Error = variation + deviation; with variation 0° the whole 3°E error is deviation on this heading.

fig.title: Compass check on the agonic line

q: Your watches have stopped and you know UT only to about 20 minutes. Which compass check can you still make?
a: The Sun's amplitude at sunrise or sunset
o: The Sun's azimuth in mid-morning
A star's azimuth at evening twilight
A planet's azimuth in the night
why: The amplitude needs only the Dec, which changes slowly; an azimuth needs the hour angle, and so the exact time.

fig.title: No reliable time
lines: Deck watch and GPS both dead
UT known only to about ±20 min
